summary: This RFC describes the Exterior Gateway Protocol used to connect stub gateways to an autonomous system of core gateways. It specifies the working protocol and defines it as an official ARPA protocol. It is an early stage in how Internet routing between systems developed.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes how a stub gateway connects its local networks to core gateways. It defines a handshake, reachability checks, and a polling exchange for reporting which networks can be reached through a gateway.

questions: what is the stub exterior gateway protocol
how did stub gateways connect to the core
how do egp neighbors check reachability
what is an egp network reachability message
subtitle: How stub gateways exchange neighbor and network reachability information with core gateways.

tldr.problem: A single routing algorithm across a growing Internet would create increasing overhead and make maintenance harder.
tldr.mechanism: EGP lets a stub gateway acquire core neighbors, check that they are reachable, and answer polls with networks for which it is an appropriate first hop.
tldr.outcome: RFC 888 defines an official ARPA protocol for connecting stub gateways to the core; the unit metadata lists RFC 904 as an update.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 888 as updated by RFC 904. RFC 888 was published in January 1984 and describes the working ARPA protocol at that time.

sections.title: Stub Gateways and Autonomous Systems
sections.content:
The RFC argues that one routing algorithm shared by every gateway becomes difficult to scale, maintain, and change as the Internet grows. It describes the Internet as a set of autonomous systems, each with its own internal routing arrangements.

This document covers stub gateways that connect local networks to the core system. A stub is the only path from the core to the networks behind it, and it does not carry traffic that neither originates in nor is destined for those networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of requiring every gateway to use one shared routing method, the RFC separates the network into systems. It explains how a small stub system connects to the core.

sections.title: Acquiring and Checking Neighbors
sections.content:
Two gateways become direct neighbors through a two-way Neighbor Acquisition exchange. A gateway sends a request and receives a reply or refusal. A gateway can later send a Neighbor Cease message to end the relationship.

To check reachability, a gateway sends Hello messages and expects an I Heard You response. The RFC leaves the exact thresholds and sending frequency to the gateways and their network. A neighbor that becomes unreachable may become reachable again without repeating acquisition.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateways first agree to become neighbors. They then exchange Hello and I Heard You messages to check whether the connection still works.

sections.title: Network Reachability and Polling
sections.content:
A gateway is an appropriate first hop to a network when it can forward traffic for that network without first passing through another gateway on the shared network. A Network Reachability (NR) message lists the networks for which the sender is an appropriate first hop and gives a distance for each.

NR messages are normally sent in response to a poll. A gateway must not poll more often than once per minute. The poll and response use a sequence number to match them, and a gateway that receives no response after its retries should assume the neighbor is not an appropriate first hop for any network.
sections.plainLanguage: A poll asks which networks can be reached through a neighbor. The reply lists those networks, and the polling gateway uses that information to decide where to forward traffic.

sections.title: Indirect Neighbors and Limits
sections.content:
A gateway can learn about other gateways through the neighbor lists in NR messages. It may forward traffic directly to one of these indirect neighbors without performing acquisition, reachability checks, or polling with that gateway.

The RFC states that EGP is not itself a routing algorithm. Its information is sufficient for the stub model described here, but if the network topology does not follow those rules, EGP may not provide enough information to prevent loops. A false claim that a gateway is an appropriate first hop can also prevent traffic from reaching its destination.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway can use information from a direct neighbor to learn about other possible next hops. It must not treat EGP as a complete routing algorithm for network shapes outside the stub model.
